class: T4 microbenchmark (isolated split values kernel, S=40000; data accumulation, no e2e, no ceiling claim)
question: the integrated split values kernel (1.17x e2e) -- is it DRAM-bandwidth-bound, and can ILP reordering close the gap?
conclusions: the split values kernel is NOT DRAM-bandwidth-bound: it runs at 62 GB/s (34% of the 182.7 GB/s ceiling) on its 1x V volume.
the same access pattern with NO FMA (pure read into smem) reaches 105 GB/s (58%), so the access pattern itself is not the limit either.
ILP-2 / ILP-4 reordering (independent accumulators to break the serial FMA dependency) does NOT help (1.320 -> 1.323 ms): the remaining overhead is not the serial FMA chain.
the 0.542 ms/layer gap between the pure-read version (0.778) and the full kernel (1.320) is FMA + probability-load + partial-store overhead that ILP does not remove.
implication: the integrated split values path (165.2 ms/step e2e) is close to where this kernel design will land; further micro-optimization of this kernel is low-yield. The dominant remaining decode cost is the weight-read GEMV kernels (100.52 ms/step, 38% of the step, already at the DRAM ceiling), which require a different lever (batching, lower quantization, or a target re-set) and owner adjudication.
e2e: not run for the ILP variants -- the microbenchmark shows no improvement, so there is no e2e candidate to validate.
evidence: isolated microbenchmark (sources removed after use per /tmp hygiene)
